claims.statement: From 2 August 2026, EU AI Act transparency rules require covered chatbots to tell users they are interacting with AI and require labels or machine-readable marks for covered generated or altered content.
Regression monitoring is a recurring operational need rather than a one-time legal memo for firms that ship interface and model changes frequently.
The exact number of Polish deployers in scope and their budget for a standalone scanner are unknown.

contrary_evidence: Model and platform vendors may build default labels and provenance marks into their products.
Whether a particular system or item is legally covered can require contextual legal analysis that a scanner cannot replace.
Generic accessibility, privacy and AI-governance scanners can add similar checks.

economics.acquisition_route: Identify prospects from public chatbot surfaces, offer a concise evidence-based audit through web and software agencies, and let agencies resell the monitor across client portfolios.
economics.founder_time: Part-time validation hypothesis; delivery burden remains untested.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: A test library across frameworks, languages and content formats can improve coverage and reduce false alarms. Regulations and codes are public, so execution reliability rather than data accumulation would be the advantage.
fingerprint.customer: Polish SaaS companies, agencies and mid-market firms deploying customer-facing chatbots or automated synthetic-content pipelines in the EU.
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: Identify prospects from public chatbot surfaces, offer a concise evidence-based audit through web and software agencies, and let agencies resell the monitor across client portfolios.
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: Crawl only authorized public test paths, inspect disclosure language and machine-readable metadata, run scripted interaction checks, retain dated screenshots or response evidence, and route legal-scope questions to counsel. Sell a fixed audit first and recurring monitoring second.
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: The deployer or its digital agency pays for an initial public-surface audit and a monthly regression monitor when the service records a change, missing disclosure or broken mark and produces an evidence snapshot.
fingerprint.problem_trigger: A chatbot, model, interface or content pipeline changes and the owner needs continuing evidence that users receive the required AI disclosure and generated or altered media carries the expected labels or machine-readable marks.

founder_fit: Direct fit with AI systems, automated testing and evidence capture
Public-surface audits are part-time-testable without deep integration
Agency resale reduces repeated high-energy sales
No personal brand or camera presence is needed
risks: Evidence of a workflow, transition, or loss does not yet establish recurring willingness to pay.
The proposed distribution and compounding mechanisms remain hypotheses pending buyer evidence.

title: AI Act transparency regression scanner for chatbots and synthetic media
uncertainties: Machine-readable formats and browser-observable tests accepted in practice
National enforcement priorities and demand outside high-profile use cases
False-positive rates across Polish language interfaces
Agency willingness to resell rather than build simple checks internally
Pricing, buyer authority, and acquisition economics remain unvalidated at discovery.

First validation test: With authorization, audit 30 public Polish chatbot or synthetic-content surfaces, provide ten deployers a one-page finding, and offer a paid 60-day regression monitor. Require three paid monitors and at least one detected post-deployment regression before expanding to broader AI governance.
